ai.definition: Bioelectricity harnesses the electrical energy generated by certain organisms, such as electric eels, through their specialized cells called electrocytes.
ai.howItWorks: Electrocyte cells in electric eels pump ions to create an electrical potential. When triggered, these cells discharge simultaneously, producing a high-voltage shock similar to that of a battery.
ai.problemSolved: Demonstrates the feasibility and principles behind biological power generation for energy applications.
ai.manufacturing: Not applicable at this stage; purely based on natural phenomena in electric eels.
ai.costDrivers: None, as it is a naturally occurring phenomenon.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Potential for future development but currently limited to basic understanding and demonstration.
ai.regulation: No specific regulations apply at this stage of research.
ai.risks: Limited; primarily theoretical and experimental risks in studying the mechanisms involved.
ai.profitability: Not applicable, as it is a concept at this stage.
ai.futureDevelopment: Research into mimicking natural bioelectricity for energy generation or medical applications.

glossary.def: The use of electricity generated by biological organisms.
Specialized cells in electric eels that generate electrical energy through ion pumping.

subsystems.name: Electrocyte cells
subsystems.role: the voltage-generating unit — flattened cells that pump ions across their membranes to build a charge.

subsystems.name: Series stack
subsystems.role: thousands of cells stacked like battery cells in series, so small voltages add up to hundreds of volts.

subsystems.name: Discharge control
subsystems.role: nerves fire the cells almost simultaneously, so the stack discharges as one pulse rather than dribbling out.

subsystems.name: Power interface
subsystems.role: the output — in water, current flows between the head and tail; in an engineered device, electrodes take it out.

subsystems.name: Metabolic supply
subsystems.role: the living part of the system, which must be fed and kept alive to keep pumping ions.

subsystems.name: Engineered analogue
subsystems.role: artificial versions replace cells with hydrogels and ion-selective membranes to avoid keeping tissue alive.

buildSteps.title: Choose the mechanism
buildSteps.detail: Either culture real electrocyte-like cells, or copy the trick with synthetic ion-selective membranes — the first is biological, the second is engineering.

buildSteps.title: Grow or lay down the membranes
buildSteps.detail: Cells are cultured on scaffolds; in the synthetic route, cationic and anionic hydrogel compartments are patterned side by side.

buildSteps.title: Stack the units in series
buildSteps.detail: Repeating membrane pairs are layered like cells in a battery pack so their voltages add; a few millivolts per unit only becomes useful at hundreds or thousands of repeats.

buildSteps.title: Wire and seal
buildSteps.detail: End electrodes are attached, and the stack is encapsulated in a flexible, watertight, ion-tight housing that still lets the internal chemistry work.

buildSteps.title: Trigger the discharge
buildSteps.detail: A control circuit or nerve-like signal fires the stack in one coordinated pulse, since the power comes from the burst, not a steady trickle.

buildSteps.title: Characterise output
buildSteps.detail: Voltage, current and pulse duration are measured — biological systems give high voltage but modest current, so the energy per pulse is small.

buildSteps.title: Feed and maintain
buildSteps.detail: For living versions, supply nutrients, oxygen and a comfortable temperature, and remove waste; this upkeep is the main practical burden.

buildSteps.title: Integrate with a load
buildSteps.detail: Connect to a sensor, implant or microdevice, with capacitors or converters that smooth the pulsed output into something usable.

prerequisites.why: the whole effect comes from pumping ions against a gradient; without this knowledge there is nothing to copy.
living power sources need electrocyte-like cells kept alive and organised in the right geometry.
they allow the same voltage stacking without living tissue.

prerequisites.tech: Bioelectrochemical systems and microbial fuel cells
prerequisites.why: bacteria can already generate small currents from organic matter, demonstrated in wastewater pilots but at low power density.
anything implanted must survive the body and not harm it, which limits materials and lifetime.

pathway.milestone: laboratory studies of electrocytes and artificial stacks — a 2017 Nature paper demonstrated a soft power source of stacked hydrogels and ion-selective membranes reaching on the order of 100 volts
pathway.unlocks: understanding of how to build voltage in series from soft, wet materials.

pathway.milestone: engineered tissues that power microdevices — sensors, lab-on-chip systems or small implants
pathway.unlocks: devices that need no battery replacement because they harvest their own chemistry.

pathway.milestone: bioelectrochemical systems integrated into wastewater treatment and bioreactors
pathway.unlocks: small amounts of electricity recovered while treating waste.

pathway.milestone: self-powered medical implants and biodegradable power sources
pathway.unlocks: a niche where biology beats batteries, since biological power is inherently low-current and unsuited to grid-scale supply.
